name: Burmese
sources: Watkins, Justin W. (2001). Burmese. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 31(2), 291-295.
Wheatley, Julian K. (1987). Burmese. In Bernard Comrie (ed.), The World's Major Languages. Croom Helm.
Okell, John (1969). A Reference Grammar of Colloquial Burmese. Oxford University Press.
Green, Antony D. (2005). Word, foot, and syllable structure in Burmese. In Justin Watkins (ed.), Studies in Burmese Linguistics. Pacific Linguistics.
Bradley, David (1982). Register in Burmese. In David Bradley (ed.), Papers in South-East Asian Linguistics 8: Tonation. Pacific Linguistics.
Thein Tun (1982). Some acoustic properties of tones in Burmese. In David Bradley (ed.), Papers in South-East Asian Linguistics 8: Tonation. Pacific Linguistics.
Gruber, James F. (2011). An Articulatory, Acoustic, and Auditory Study of Burmese Tone. PhD dissertation, Georgetown University.
Watkins, Justin (2000). Notes on creaky and killed tone in Burmese. SOAS Working Papers in Linguistics 10.
Bhaskararao, Peri & Ladefoged, Peter (1991). Two types of voiceless nasals. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 21(2), 80-88.
Jenny, Mathias & San San Hnin Tun (2016). Burmese: A Comprehensive Grammar. Routledge.
contrasts: four tones that combine pitch, voice quality, duration and vowel quality: low, high, creaky, checked
three-way laryngeal contrast in stops and affricates: voiceless unaspirated, voiceless aspirated, voiced
voiced against voiceless sonorants: m m̥, n n̥, ɲ ɲ̊, ŋ ŋ̊, l l̥ (and rare w ʍ)
plain against aspirated fricative, s against sʰ (merging for some speakers)
oral open rhymes, nasalised rhymes and rhymes closed by a glottal stop
full (major) syllables against reduced (minor) syllables with ə
allophony: the only codas are a glottal stop and a placeless nasal; the written final stops k, c, t, p are all a glottal stop, and the written final nasals are all nasalisation of the vowel
the final nasal is realised as a nasalised vowel, with a weak nasal closure that takes the place of a following stop
in close juncture the final glottal stop assimilates completely to the next consonant, giving a long stop

voicing sandhi: inside a word or a close-knit phrase, voiceless unaspirated and aspirated obstruents become voiced after a syllable that ends in a vowel or a nasal, but not after a glottal stop (the particle tɛ̀ is [dɛ̀] after an open or nasal syllable)
voiceless nasals are voiceless for most of their length and end in a short voiced part before the vowel (Bhaskararao & Ladefoged 1991)
θ is a dental stop or affricate [t̪ ~ t̪θ] more often than a fricative; its voiced partner ð appears in voicing sandhi
vowels in closed syllables differ from those in open syllables: i and u are lowered and centralised to [ɪ] and [ʊ], and the diphthongs ei, ai, au, ou take the place of the mid monophthongs e, o, ɔ
ə occurs only in minor syllables
ɹ occurs only in loanwords (Pali, English) and names
syllable_structure: major syllable C(G)V(N or ʔ) plus tone, where G is j or w; minor syllable Cə without tone or coda
phonotactics: a minor syllable is never final in a word: it is always followed by a major syllable, so words are iambic (sesquisyllabic)
minor syllables have a single consonant onset, the vowel ə, no coda and no tone
the checked tone occurs only in syllables closed by a glottal stop; the other three tones only in open and nasal syllables
the diphthongs ei ai au ou occur only in closed (nasal or glottal) syllables
medial j follows labials only; older velar plus j are now the palatal affricates
voiceless sonorants occur only as onsets

stress.type: no contrastive stress; major versus minor syllables
stress.rule: Major syllables are prominent and carry tone, minor syllables are weak; the last major syllable of a word is the strongest.
stress.cues: duration, full vowel quality and tone on major syllables; short ə and no tone on minor syllables

rhythm.vowel_reduction: strong in minor syllables: any vowel becomes ə, the syllable loses its coda and its tone and is short
rhythm.notes: Iambic pattern of weak minor and strong major syllables (Green 2005). Syllable duration also depends on the tone.

length.notes: No separate length contrast: duration is part of the tone. Checked syllables are the shortest and creaky syllables are short; low and high syllables are long, the high tone usually being described as the longest (Wheatley 1987). Long consonants arise only when a final glottal stop assimilates to the next consonant.

intonation.declarative: lexical tones are kept; declination; statements usually end in a particle with its own tone (tɛ̀, mɛ̀, pì)
intonation.yes_no_question: marked by the final particle lá (high tone); no separate rising melody is needed
intonation.wh_question: marked by the final particle lɛ́ (high tone) with the question word in place
intonation.continuation: non-final clauses end in subordinating particles; the high tone stays high instead of falling when more follows
intonation.notes: Burmese intonation has been little studied instrumentally; the entries are general.

tone.confidence_notes: The four-way system and its cues are well established (medium to high confidence). The Chao digits are the compiler's approximation of published prose descriptions (Wheatley 1987; Watkins 2001), which give pitch in words, not numerals. The main pitch division is low against the other three; high, creaky and checked are all in the upper register and differ mostly in voice quality and duration.

inventory.name: low tone (also called level)
inventory.description: Low level, often rising slightly at the end before a pause.

inventory.name: high tone (also called heavy)
inventory.description: High, with a fall at the end before a pause.
inventory.connected_speech: high level or slightly rising, without the fall, when another syllable follows in the phrase

inventory.name: creaky tone
inventory.description: High and falling, short, with tense or creaky voice and a weak glottal closure at the end.
inventory.connected_speech: high, short; the glottal closure weakens before another syllable
inventory.phonation: creaky or tense, often with a lax final glottal stop

inventory.name: checked tone (also called killed or stopped)
inventory.description: High and very short, ending in an abrupt glottal stop; the vowel is centralised or diphthongised.
inventory.connected_speech: very short; the glottal stop assimilates to a following consonant; pitch can vary with context
inventory.phonation: modal, cut off by the glottal stop

sandhi: minor syllables have no tone: a full syllable that is reduced to a minor syllable loses its tone along with its vowel quality and coda (tiʔ 'one' is tə before a classifier, n̥iʔ 'two' is n̥ə)
the high tone falls only before a pause; inside a phrase it stays high
induced creaky tone: a low or high tone word takes the creaky tone in some grammatical contexts, such as the possessive (ŋà 'I', ŋa̰ 'my'); this is grammatical, not phonological
voicing sandhi and assimilation of the final glottal stop affect the consonants between syllables, not the tones
tone.neutral_tone: Minor syllables (consonant plus ə) are toneless, short and weak; their pitch is low to mid and follows from the neighbouring syllables.
tone.notes: Instrumental studies (Thein Tun 1982; Watkins 2000, 2001; Gruber 2011) agree that the low tone has the lowest pitch and modal voice, that the creaky tone is short with creaky voice and falling pitch, and that the checked tone is the shortest and ends in a full glottal stop. No absolute F0 or duration values are given here.

phonation: creaky or tense voice on the creaky tone
slightly breathy voice on the high tone for some speakers
final glottal stop on the checked tone

problems: dictsource/my_rules maps letters one by one with no syllable parsing and supplies no inherent vowel after a bare consonant, so most words come out as strings of consonants (မြန်မာ gives [mrn mts], မင်္ဂလာပါ gives [mŋ ɡltspe])
the vowel sign aa is turned into the consonant cluster ts

tone is not assigned by rule: only a few vowel signs carry a fixed tone digit (ii and uu tone 1, u and e tone 3, visarga tone 2); the creaky dot below and the asat are turned into a short pause, and the tokenizer ends the word at them

Burmese is not flagged as a tone language in src/libespeak-ng/tr_languages.c (the my case only disables numbers), so CalcPitches_Tone() is not used; tone phonemes give a contour shape but pitch levels come from the default stress-based intonation

the tone definitions do not match the language: low (1) and checked (4) have the same rise-fall contour, high (2) is a wide rise and creaky (3) a dip followed by a rise; none has creaky or breathy voice or a glottal closure
the vowel phonemes of ph_myanmar (a01 to a50, one for each written rhyme) are not used by my_rules, which call generic vowels of the base table
no voiceless nasals or lateral (ha-hto is mapped to h plus a), no aspirated fricative, no palatal affricates; θ is mapped to the voiced fricative D
written final stops are not turned into a glottal stop, final nasals are not turned into nasalisation, and there is no voicing sandhi and no reduction to minor syllables
numbers are disabled in tr_languages.c although my_list has the digits
the result is not intelligible as Burmese
good: nothing that reaches the listener yet; the phoneme table does contain recorded Burmese consonants and tone-dependent vowel lengths for six vowels (low longest at about 410 to 470, high 300 to 345, checked and creaky about 170 to 270), which could be used once the rules are written

notes: eSpeak NG tone phonemes in ph_myanmar: 1 low, 2 high, 3 creaky, 4 checked. The vowel lengths in ph_myanmar make the low tone the longest, while Wheatley's description gives the high tone as the longest; the literature is not unanimous on this point.
